# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–27 (Complete – Updated 194)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn in continental Europe, seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now established in Pumpernickel (a small German principality) for autumn/winter season.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; **Pumpernickel** (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Prime Minister's lodgings, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey, Saint Michael's Fountain, Artillery Place, Stadthaus, Town Hall, Redoute, gardens with Trophonius' cave, nymphbath, Niagara cataract); Mirecombe; Dunholt; Dunwick; Quenwick; Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; Ems; Aix-la-Chapelle; Baden-Baden; Salwick; Elephant (lodging-house); Boulogne (French coast refuge); Albion/England; Salmere.

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)
Amelia nursed father devotedly during final illness. Old Sedley forgave past grievances, confessing unkindness to Amelia. Died peacefully in sleep. Buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife. Major Dobbin, Jos, and Georgy followed remains to grave.

## Mr. Osborne's Stroke and Death (Chapter 26)
Osborne's mind visibly changing in final months. Asked Georgy about Jos; invited Jos and Dobbin to dinner where every family plate was exhibited. Osborne asked Dobbin repeatedly about Mrs. George Osborne. Dobbin spoke eloquently of Amelia's sufferings, passionate attachment to husband's memory, tender duty to parents, sacrifice of boy. Osborne replied: "By God, you are a good feller, sir." Reconciliation meeting never took place. Old Sedley's lingering illness intervened. Osborne found in dressing-room at foot of dressing-table in fit. Pocket of dressing-gown contained letter from George written from Waterloo and key to box of son's papers; seals broken—likely read night before seizure while reading great red family Bible in study. Died in four days without speaking again.

**Will Terms**: Half property left to George Osborne (minor); remainder between two sisters. Mr. Bullock to continue commercial house affairs. **Annuity**: Five hundred pounds, chargeable on George's property, left to Amelia, "the widow of my beloved son, George Osborne," who was to resume guardianship of boy. Major William Dobbin appointed executor, named "my beloved son's friend." Will stated Osborne maintained grandson and widow "when they were otherwise without means of support" and bequeathed sum "sufficient to purchase his commission as a Lieutenant-Colonel, or to be disposed of in any way he may think fit." Will showed "the hatred which he had so long cherished had gone out of his heart."

## Amelia's Transformation and New Life (Chapter 26)
Upon learning of William's bounty supporting her in poverty, Amelia "sank on her knees, and prayed for blessings on that constant and kind heart." Visited deserted Gaunt House in deep sables. Found straw littered in front, great blank rooms bearing marks where pictures and mirrors hung. At George's upper room window (where she once gazed as child), looked out over Russell Square toward her birthplace. Thought of "man who had been her constant protector, her good genius, her sole benefactor, her tender and generous friend." Took temporary house at Richmond. During continental tour, discovered Dobbin's true gentlemanly character—generous aims, constant truth, elevated degree, lack of meanness making him simple, honest face, warm and humble heart. "Emmy, in this happy time, found that hers underwent a very great change in respect of the merits of the Major."

## Continental Tour (Chapter 26)
Party landed Rotterdam, traveled by steamer to Cologne. Jos announced arrival in Cologne newspapers as "Herr Graf Lord von Sedley nebst Begleitung aus London." Had court dress; insisted Dobbin bring regimental paraphernalia; announced intention to be presented at foreign courts. Left own card and Major's on "Our Minister" wherever party stopped. Kept journal noting defects or excellences of inns and wines. Observed Earl of Bareacres and family on ship; both "looked rather younger" than remembered from Brussels in '15, with Lady's dark hair now "a beautiful golden auburn" and Lord's red whiskers now "of a rich black with purple and green reflections." Amelia very happy and pleased. Dobbin carried her stool and sketch-book, admired her drawings. She sat upon steamers' decks and drew crags and castles, or mounted upon donkeys to ascend ancient robber-towers, attended by Georgy and Dobbin. She laughed at Major's droll figure on donkey-back with long legs touching ground. "Perhaps it was the happiest time of both their lives...this couple were very decently contented, and enjoyed as pleasant a summer tour as any pair that left England that year."

## Pumpernickel Arrival and Society (Chapter 26–27)
**Theatre and British Recognition**: Party attended theatre. Upon "burst of that beloved and well-known music," every Englishman in house proclaimed membership in British nation—"Sir John and Lady Bullminster (who had taken a house at Pumpernickel for the education of their nine children), the fat gentleman with the mustachios, the long Major in white duck trousers, and the lady with the little boy." Tapeworm, Charge d'Affaires (nephew and heir of old Marshal Tiptoff, now deceased), rose in his box and bowed.

**Tapeworm's Attentions**: Near end of performance, Tapeworm approached Jos with "fascinating smile" and invitation to stay in Pumpernickel. Accepted Jos's invitation to lodge at his quarters. Put dexterous questions to Jos about India and dancing-girls; asked Amelia about "that beautiful boy" (Georgy); complimented her upon "prodigious sensation which she had made in the house"; tried to fascinate Dobbin talking of late war and Pumpernickel contingent exploits. Doctor von Glauber speedily convinced Jos that Pumpernickel mineral springs and Doctor's particular treatment would "infallibly restore the Bengalee to youth and slimness." Jos's mind made up; committed to spend autumn in Pumpernickel. Next day, Tapeworm presented Jos and Major to Victor Aurelius XVII, conducted by Count de Schlusselback, Marshal of the Court. Straightway invited to dinner at Court. Upon announcement of intention to stay, "politest ladies of the whole town instantly called upon Mrs. Osborne"; as not one was under rank of Baroness, "Jos's delight was beyond expression." **Advancement**: Tapeworm's transparent (representing young Couple advancing and Discord flying away, with ludicrous likeness to French Ambassador) beat French picture hollow; likely got Tapeworm the advancement and the Cross of the Bath which he subsequently attained.

**Emmy at Court and Evening Dress**: Emmy presented to august family. On certain days mourning not admitted at Court, so she appeared in pink crape dress with diamond ornament in corsage presented by her brother. "She looked so pretty in this costume that the Duke and Court (putting out of the question the Major, who had scarcely ever seen her before in an evening dress, and vowed that she did not look five-and-twenty) all admired her excessively."

**Pumpernickel Government and Society**: Constitution moderate despotism tempered by Chamber that might or might not be elected. Prime Minister lodged in second floor; Foreign Secretary occupied comfortable lodgings over Zwieback's Conditorey. Army consisted of magnificent band that also did duty on stage. Noble society divided into factions: Strumpff faction (supported by Tapeworm, English) and Lederlung party (supported by French Charge d'Affaires M. de Macabau). Politics ran very high; parties very bitter. Strumpff was greater singer, stout, not in first youth and beauty; Lederlung pretty creature with sweet voice. Two women were "two flags of the French and the English party at Pumpernickel." French party included Foreign Minister, Commander-in-Chief's Lady (who served under Napoleon), Hof-Marschall and his wife. English party included Home Minister, Master of the Horse, Duke's Private Secretary, Prince's Tutor. Secretary of French Chancery was little Grignac, young fellow, malicious, made caricatures of Tapeworm in albums of place. Theatre known and famous in that quarter of Germany. Present Duke in youth insisted upon having his own operas played there; one day in fury from orchestra place broke bassoon on Chapel Master's head, leading too slow. Duchess Sophia wrote domestic comedies. Prince executes music in private now; Duchess gives away her plays to foreigners of distinction. Court conducted with comfort and splendour. When balls held with four hundred people at supper, servant in scarlet and lace attended upon every four; all served on silver. Festivals and entertainments going continually on. Gardens arranged to emulate those of Versailles; allegorical waterworks include Trophonius' cave with leaden Tritons spouting water and playing groans from lead conchs, nymphbath, Niagara cataract.

**Emmy's Social Activities (Chapter 27)**: Before winter far advanced, Emmy took night and received company with great propriety and modesty. Had French master who complimented her upon purity of accent and facility of learning; she had learned long ago and grounded herself subsequently in grammar to teach George. Madam Strumpff came to give her lessons in singing, performed so well with such true voice that Major's windows opposite (lodgings under Prime Minister) were always open to hear lesson. German ladies, very sentimental and simple, fell in love with her and called her du at once. Major made himself George's tutor, read Caesar and mathematics with him; they had German master and rode out of evenings by side of Emmy's carriage. Emmy too timid, made dreadful outcry at slightest disturbance on horse-back. Drove about with one of dear German friends, Jos asleep on back-seat of barouche.

## Georgy Osborne (Chapter 26–27)
Now eleven years old; boy's "quick brain" revealed grandfather "a dullard." Day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. On continental tour: walked ahead during excursions, climbing towers and trees, while Amelia and Dobbin walked soberly below. Made "prodigious advance in the knowledge of High Dutch" conversing with Herr Kirsch on carriage box. Now heir to half Osborne's substantial property. Will restored him to mother's guardianship. Boy remained active, imperious, good-natured.

**At Pumpernickel Wedding Festivities (Chapter 27)**: Got sausage wrenching it off pole at games during wedding festivities of Hereditary Prince of Pumpernickel with Princess Amelia of Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; gave sausage to peasant standing at foot of mast. **At Gambling**: With relations away at Court festival, Georgy came to Stadthaus Ball with uncle's courier Kirsch. Hankered round roulette and trente-et-quarante tables (only allowed for week of festivities). Major Dobbin instantly went up to Georgy and pulled him briskly back from place of temptation, showing him eloquently why he shouldn't be there, would have enforced precepts by example of Georgy's own father, had he liked to say anything reflecting on other's memory. Major then housed him and went to bed, noting when his light in little room outside Amelia's presently disappeared.

## Jos's Activities at Pumpernickel (Chapter 27)
**Romantic Interest**: Jos becoming very sweet upon Grafinn Fanny de Butterbrod, very gentle tender-hearted and unassuming young creature, a Canoness and Countess in her own right but with scarcely ten pounds per year to her fortune. Fanny declared that to be Amelia's sister was greatest delight Heaven could bestow. Jos might have put Countess's shield and coronet by side of own arms on carriage and forks.

**At Gambling**: At Stadthaus, Jos remained behind over play-table; no gambler but not averse to little excitement of sport now and then, had some Napoleons chinking in embroidered pockets of court waistcoat. Put down one over fair shoulder of little gambler before him, and they won. Woman made little movement to make room for him, took skirt of gown from vacant chair. Jos sat down. Woman said archly: "Come and give me good luck," in foreign accent. Jos replied about winning and giving fortune. She asked if he played much; Jos said: "Yes; ay nap after dinner." Woman continued in pretty French accent, revealing knowledge of Georgy as image of his father, noting Jos's changes, lamenting her own unhappiness. Mentioned seeing "dear Amelia" that day, how pretty and happy she looked. Revealed herself as **Rebecca (Madame de Raudon)**, formerly involved with Rawdon Crawley.

## Rebecca/Becky's Degradation and Current State (Chapter 27)
**Moral Decline**: "This abattement and degradation did not take place all at once; it was brought about by degrees, after her calamity, and after many struggles to keep up--as a man who goes overboard hangs on to a spar whilst any hope is left, and then flings it away and goes down, when he finds that struggling is in vain." **Period of despair**: "There was period in Mrs. Becky's life when she was seized, not by remorse, but by kind of despair, and absolutely neglected her person and did not even care for her reputation."

**After Curzon Street Catastrophe and Duel**: Lingered in London while Rawdon prepared for departure to Coventry Island. Made more than one attempt to see Sir Pitt Crawley and work upon his feelings, which she had almost enlisted in her favour. Spied by Wenham in black veil lurking near palace of legislature; sneaked away when their eyes met; never succeeded in designs upon Baronet. Probably Lady Jane interposed. Lady Jane quite astonished husband by spirit exhibited, determination to disown Becky. Of her own movement, invited Rawdon to come and stop in Gaunt Street until his departure for Coventry Island, knowing him for guard Mrs. Becky would not try to force her door; looked curiously at superscriptions of all letters arrived for Sir Pitt, lest he and his sister-in-law correspond. Rebecca did not try to see or write to Pitt at his own house, and after one or two attempts consented to his demand that correspondence regarding conjugal differences should be carried on by lawyers only.

**Wenham's Poisoning of Pitt's Mind**: Short time after Lord Steyne's accident, Wenham gave Baronet biography of Mrs. Becky astonishing member for Queen's Crawley. He knew everything regarding her: who her father was; in what year her mother danced at opera; what had been her previous history; and what her conduct during married life. Though greater part of story likely false and dictated by interested malevolence, Becky left with "sad sad reputation in the esteem of a country gentleman and relative who had been once rather partial to her."

**Financial Settlement**: Revenues of Governor of Coventry Island not large. Part set aside by Rawdon for payment of outstanding debts and liabilities; charges incident on his situation required considerable expense; found he could not spare to his wife more than three hundred pounds a year, proposed to pay on undertaking she would never trouble him. Otherwise, scandal, separation, Doctors' Commons would ensue. Wenham, Steyne, Rawdon, everybody's business to get her out of country and hush up disagreeable affair.

**Boulogne Refuge (Chapter 27)**: First flight not very far. Perched upon French coast at Boulogne, refuge of so much exiled English innocence. Lived in rather genteel, widowed manner with femme de chambre and couple of rooms at hotel. Dined at table d'hote where people thought her very pleasant. Entertained neighbours by stories of brother Sir Pitt and great London acquaintance, talking easy, fashionable slip-slop having much effect upon certain folks of small breeding. Passed with many for person of importance. Gave little tea-parties in private room and shared in innocent amusements of place in sea-bathing, jaunts in open carriages, strolls on sands, visits to play. Mrs. Burjoice, printer's lady, voted her charming until little rogue Burjoice began paying too much attention. Becky always affable, easy, good-natured—especially with men.

**Social Rejection at Boulogne**: Numbers of people going abroad as usual at end of season; Becky found out by behaviour of acquaintances opinion of "society" regarding her conduct. One day confronted Lady Partlet and daughters walking modestly on Boulogne pier. Lady Partlet marshalled all daughters round her with sweep of parasol and retreated from pier, darting savage glances at poor Becky who stood alone. On another day, Lady Slingstone arrived by packet, exceedingly ill in carriage, greatly exhausted. All her energies rallied instant she saw Becky smiling under pink bonnet; Lady Slingstone gave glance of scorn such as would have shrivelled up most women, walked into Custom House quite unsupported. Becky only laughed; but "I don't think she liked it. She felt she was alone, quite alone, and the far-off shining cliffs of England were impassable to her."

**Male Behaviour Changed**: Behaviour of men underwent change. Grinstone showed his teeth and laughed in her face with familiarity not pleasant. Little Bob Suckling, who was cap in hand to her three months before and would walk mile in rain to see her carriage at Gaunt House, talking to Fitzoof of Guards (Lord Heehaw's son) on jetty nodded to her over his shoulder without moving his hat. Tom Raikes tried to walk into her sitting-room at inn with cigar in mouth; she closed door upon him, would have locked it only his fingers were inside. "She felt very lonely indeed. 'If HE'D been here,' she said, 'those cowards would never have dared to insult me.' She thought about 'him' with great sadness and perhaps longing--about his honest, stupid, constant kindness and fidelity; his never-ceasing obedience; his good humour; his bravery and courage." **Plan**: Very likely she cried, for she was particularly lively and had put on little extra rouge when came down to dinner.

**Women's Sympathy Worse Than Male Insults**: Perhaps insults of men not so intolerable as sympathy of certain women. Mrs. Crackenbury and Mrs. Washington White passed through Boulogne on way to Switzerland, protected by Colonel Horner, young Beaumoris, old Crackenbury, and Mrs. White's little girl. They did not avoid her. They giggled, cackled, tattled, condoled, consoled, and patronized her until drove her almost wild with rage. "To be patronized by THEM! she thought, as they went away simpering after kissing her." She heard Beaumoris's laugh ringing on stair and knew quite well how to interpret his hilarity.

## Other Reconciliations (Chapter 26)
Mrs. Frederick Bullock, "although despoiled by that little monster of one-half of the sum which she expected from her father, nevertheless showed her charitableness of spirit by being reconciled to the mother and the boy." One day chariot with golden bullocks emblazoned on panels drove to Amelia's house. Bullock family made irruption into garden where Amelia was reading, Jos in arbour dipping strawberries into wine, Major in Indian jacket giving back to Georgy for jumping over him. Those ladies met "after an absence of more than fifteen years." Per Rowdy and Hollyock's conversation, Mrs. Bullock "is always scheming and managing. She wants Mrs. Osborne's account to be taken from our house to hers--and the way in which she coaxes that boy and makes him sit by that blear-eyed little Rosa is perfectly ridiculous." Miss Swartz and husband came thundering over from Hampton Court with flaming yellow liveries, "as impetuously fond of Amelia as ever."

## Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 23–24)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation: maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education, compensates wronged. Separated from Rebecca permanently after duel with Steyne.
